athletism: The state or practice of an athlete; the characteristics of an athlete.
attagas: A species of sand grouse (Syrrghaptes Pallasii) found in Asia and rarely in southern Europe.
atrophy: A wasting away from want of nourishment; diminution in bulk or slow emaciation of the body or of any part. Milton. | To cause to waste away or become abortive; to starve or weaken.
atmologic: Of or pertaining to atmology. "Atmological laws of heat." Whewell.
ate: 1. As an ending of participles or participial adjectives it is equivalent to -ed; as, situate or situated; animate or animated. 2. As the ending of a verb, it means to make, to cause, to act, etc.; as, to propitiate (to make propitious); to animate (to give life to). 3. As a noun suffix, it marks the agent; as, curate, delegate. It also sometimes marks the office or dignity;
attaint: 1. To attain; to get act; to hit. (old) 2. (Old Law) To find guilty; to convict; -- said esp. of a jury on trial for giving a false verdict. (old) Upon sufficient proof attainted of some open act by… | Attainted; corrupted. (old) Shak.
atypic: That has no type; devoid of typical character; irregular; unlike the type.
atlantes: Figures or half figures of men, used as columns to support an entablature; -- called also telamones. See Caryatides. Oxf. Gloss.
attune: 1. To tune or put in tune; to make melodious; to adjust, as one sound or musical instrument to another; as, to attune the voice to a harp. 2. To arrange fitly; to make accordant. Wake to energy each social aim, Attuned spontaneous to the will of Jove. Beattie.
athleticism: The practice of engaging in athletic games; athletism.
attainable: 1. Capable of being attained or reached by efforts of the mind or body; capable of being compassed or accomplished by efforts directed to the object. The highest pitch of perfection attainable in this life. Addison. 2. Obtainable.
athwart: 1. Across; from side to side of. Athwart the thicket lone. Tennyson. 2. (Naut.) Across the direction or course of; as, a fleet standing athwart our course. Athwart hawse, across the stem of another… | 1. Across, especially in an oblique direction; sidewise; obliquely. Sometimes athwart, sometimes he strook him straight. Spenser. 2. Across the course; so as to thwart; perversely.
ataman: A hetman, or chief of the Cossacks.
atheize: To render atheistic or godless. They endeavored to atheize one another. Berkeley. | To discourse, argue, or act as an atheist. -- A"the*i`zer, n. Cudworth.
atoll: A coral island or islands, consisting of a belt of coral reef, partly submerged, surrounding a central lagoon or depression; a lagoon island.
atticism: 1. A favoring of, or attachment to, the Athenians. 2. The style and idiom of the Greek language, used by the Athenians; a concise and elegant expression.
atheistical: 1. Pertaining to, implying, or containing, atheism; -- applied to things; as, atheistic doctrines, opinions, or books. Atheistical explications of natural effects. Barrow. 2. Disbelieving the existence of a God; impious; godless; -- applied to persons; as, an atheistic writer. -- A`the*is"tic*al*ly, adv. -- A`the*is"tic*al*ness, n.
atellan: Of or pertaining to Atella, in ancient Italy; as, Atellan plays; farcical; ribald. -- n. A farcical drama performed at Atella.
attenuation: 1. The act or process of making slender, or the state of being slender; emaciation. 2. The act of attenuating; the act of making thin or less dense, or of rarefying, as fluids or gases. 3. The process of weakening in intensity; diminution of virulence; as, the attenuation of virus.
attagen: A species of sand grouse (Syrrghaptes Pallasii) found in Asia and rarely in southern Europe.
attendance: 1. Attention; regard; careful application. (old) Till I come, give attendance to reading. 1 Tim. iv. 13. 2. The act of attending; state of being in waiting; service; ministry; the fact of being present; presence. Constant attendance at church three times a day. Fielding. 3. Waiting for; expectation. (old) Languishing attendance and expectation of death. Hooker. 4.
atomic: 1. Of or pertaining to atoms. 2. Extremely minute; tiny. Atomic philosophy, or Doctrine of atoms, a system which assuming that atoms are endued with gravity and motion accounted thus for the origin and formation of all things.
ataunt: Fully rigged, as a vessel; with all sails set; set on end or set right.
athrepsia: Profound debility of children due to lack of food and to unhygienic surroundings. --A*threp"tic (#), a.
atheroma: (a) An encysted tumor containing curdy matter. (b) A disease characterized by thickening and fatty degeneration of the inner coat of the arteries.
atlantean: 1. Of or pertaining to the isle Atlantis, which the ancients allege was sunk, and overwhelmed by the ocean. 2. Pertaining to, or resembling, Atlas; strong. With Atlantean shoulders, fit to bear The weight of mightiest monarchies. Milton.
athlete: 1. (Antiq.) One who contended for a prize in the public games of ancient Greece or Rome. 2. Any one trained to contend in exercises requiring great physical agility and strength; one who has great activity and strength; a champion. 3. One fitted for, or skilled in, intellectual contests; as, athletes of debate.
athanasia: The quality of being deathless; immortality. Is not a scholiastic athanasy better than none Lowell.
atmological: Of or pertaining to atmology. "Atmological laws of heat." Whewell.
atlantides: The Pleiades or seven stars, fabled to have been the daughters of Atlas.
attractionsphere: 1. (Zoöl.) (a) The central mass of the aster in mitotic cell division; centrosphere. (b) Less often, the mass of archoplasm left by the aster in the resting cell. 2. (Bot.) A small body situated on or near the nucleus in the cells of some of the lower plants, consisting of two centrospheres containing centrosomes. It exercises an important function in mitosis.
atheneum: A temple of Athene, at Athens, in which scholars and poets were accustomed to read their works and instruct students. 2. A school founded at Rome by Hadrian. 3. A literary or scientific association or club. 4. A building or an apartment where a library, periodicals, and newspapers are kept for use.
atramentous: Of or pertaining to ink; inky; black, like ink; as, atramental galls; atramentous spots.
attorneyship: The office or profession of an attorney; agency for another. Shak.
attorneygeneral: The chief law officer of the state, empowered to act in all litigation in which the law-executing power is a party, and to advise this supreme executive whenever required. Wharton.
attractive: 1. Having the power or quality of attracting or drawing; as, the attractive force of bodies. Sir I. Newton. 2. Attracting or drawing by moral influence or pleasurable emotion; alluring; inviting; | That which attracts or draws; an attraction; an allurement. Speaks nothing but attractives and invitation. South.
attributable: Capable of being attributed; ascribable; imputable. Errors . . . attributable to carelessness. J. D. Hooker.
atrocity: 1. Enormous wickedness; extreme heinousness or cruelty. 2. An atrocious or extremely cruel deed. The atrocities which attend a victory. Macaulay.
atimy: Public disgrace or stigma; infamy; loss of civil rights. Mitford.
attainder: 1. The act of attainting, or the state of being attainted; the extinction of the civil rights and capacities of a person, consequent upon sentence of death or outlawry; as, an act of attainder. Abbott.
atrium: 1. (Arch.) (a) A square hall lighted from above, into which rooms open at one or more levels. ataxy: 1. Disorder; irregularity. (old) Bp. Hall. 2. (Med.) (a) Irregularity in disease, or in the functions. (b) The state of disorder that characterizes nervous fevers and the nervous condition. Locomotor ataxia. See Locomotor.
atmospherology: The science or a treatise on the atmosphere.
atmiatry: Treatment of disease by vapors or gases, as by inhalation.
atonable: Admitting an atonement; capable of being atoned for; expiable.
atomistic: Of or pertaining to atoms; relating to atomism. It is the object of the mechanical atomistic philosophy to confound synthesis with synartesis. Coleridge.
attractable: Capable of being attracted; subject to attraction. -- At*tract"a*ble*ness, n.
atole: A porridge or gruel of maize meal and water, milk, or the like. [Sp. Amer.]
atropism: A condition of the system produced by long use of belladonna.
attentat: 1. An attempt; an assault. (old) Bacon. 2. (Law) (a) A proceeding in a court of judicature, after an inhibition is decreed. (b) Any step wrongly innovated or attempted in a suit by an inferior judge.
atiptoe: On tiptoe; eagerly expecting. We all feel a-tiptoe with hope and confidence. F. Harrison.
atmosphere: 1. (Physics) (a) The whole mass of aëriform fluid surrounding the earth; -- applied also to the gaseous envelope of any celestial orb, or other body; as, the atmosphere of Mars. (b) Any gaseous envelope or medium. An atmosphere of cold oxygen. Miller. 2. A supposed medium around various bodies;
atrabilious: Melancholic or hypochondriac; atrabiliary. Dunglision. A hard-faced, atrabilious, earnest-eyed race. Lowell. He was constitutionally atrabilious and scornful. Froude.
atlas: 1. One who sustains a great burden. 2. (Anat.) The first vertebra of the neck, articulating immediately with the skull, thus sustaining the globe of the head, whence the name. 3. | A rich kind of satin manufactured in India. Brande & C.
attask: To take to task; to blame. Shak.
attention: 1. The act or state of attending or heeding; the application of the mind to any object of sense, representation, or thought; notice; exclusive or special consideration; earnest consideration, thought, or regard; obedient or affectionate heed; the supposed power or faculty of attending. They say the tongues of dying men Enforce attention like deep harmony. Shak.
attractor: One who, or that which, attracts. Sir T. Browne
attendancy: The quality of attending or accompanying; attendance; an attendant. (old)
attemperation: The act of attempering or regulating. (old) Bacon.
athermanous: Not transmitting heat; -- opposed to diathermanous.
atheistic: 1. Pertaining to, implying, or containing, atheism; -- applied to things; as, atheistic doctrines, opinions, or books. Atheistical explications of natural effects. Barrow. 2. Disbelieving the existence of a God; impious; godless; -- applied to persons; as, an atheistic writer. -- A`the*is"tic*al*ly, adv. -- A`the*is"tic*al*ness, n.
attraction: 1. (Physics) An invisible power in a body by which it draws anything to itself; the power in nature acting mutually between bodies or ultimate particles, tending to draw them together, or to produce their cohesion or combination, and conversely resisting separation.
attainability: The quality of being attainable; attainbleness.
atlantal: (a) Relating to the atlas. (b) Anterior; cephalic. Barclay.
atomizer: One who, or that which, atomizes; esp., an instrument for reducing a liquid to spray for disinfecting, cooling, or perfuming.
attar: A fragrant essential oil; esp., a volatile and highly fragrant essential oil obtained from the petals of roses. [Also written otto and ottar.]
athanor: A digesting furnace, formerly used by alchemists. It was so constructed as to maintain uniform and durable heat. Chambers.
attitudinarian: One who attitudinizes; a posture maker.
attributive: Attributing; pertaining to, expressing, or assigning an attribute; of the nature of an attribute. | A word that denotes an attribute; esp. a modifying word joined to a noun; an adjective or adjective phrase.
attemper: 1. To reduce, modify, or moderate, by mixture; to temper; to regulate, as temperature. If sweet with bitter . . . were not attempered still. Trench. 2. To accommodate;
attemptable: Capable of being attempted, tried, or attacked. Shak.
atazir: The influence of a star upon other stars or upon men. (old) Chaucer.
atony: Want of tone; weakness of the system, or of any organ, especially of such as are contractile.
atonic: 1. (Med.) Characterized by atony, or want of vital energy; as, an atonic disease. 2. (Gram.) Unaccented; as, an atonic syllable. 3. Destitute of tone vocality; surd. Rush. | 1. (Gram.) A word that has no accent. 2. An element of speech entirely destitute of vocality, or produced by the breath alone; a nonvocal or surd consonant; a breathing. Rush. 3.
atone: 1. In concord or friendship; in agreement (with each other); as, to be, bring, make, or set, at one, i. e., to be or bring in or to a state of agreement or reconciliation. atomize: To reduce to atoms, or to fine spray. The liquids in the form of spray are said to be pulverized, nebulized, or atomized. Dunglison.
atilt: 1. In the manner of a tilter; in the position, or with the action, of one making a thrust. "To run atilt at men." Hudibras. 2. In the position of a cask tilted, or with one end raised. atom: 1. (Physics) (a) An ultimate indivisible particle of matter. (b) An ultimate particle of matter not necessarily indivisible; a molecule. (c) A constituent particle of matter, or a molecule supposed… | To reduce to atoms. (old) Feltham.
ataxia: 1. Disorder; irregularity. (old) Bp. Hall. 2. (Med.) (a) Irregularity in disease, or in the functions. (b) The state of disorder that characterizes nervous fevers and the nervous condition. Locomotor ataxia. See Locomotor.
atheromatous: Of, pertaining to, or having the nature of, atheroma. Wiseman.
attorneyism: The practice or peculiar cleverness of attorneys.
atropine: A poisonous, white, crystallizable alkaloid, extracted from the Atropa belladonna, or deadly nightshade, and the Datura Stramonium, or thorn apple. It is remarkable for its power in dilating the pupil of the eye. Called also daturine.
athanasian: Of or pertaining to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria in the 4th century. Athanasian creed, a formulary, confession, or exposition of faith, formerly supposed to have been drawn up by Athanasius; but this opinion is now rejected, and the composition is ascribed by some to Hilary, bishop of Arles (5th century). It is a summary of what was called the orthodox faith.
athanasy: The quality of being deathless; immortality. Is not a scholiastic athanasy better than none Lowell.
athenaeum: A temple of Athene, at Athens, in which scholars and poets were accustomed to read their works and instruct students. 2. A school founded at Rome by Hadrian. 3. A literary or scientific association or club. 4. A building or an apartment where a library, periodicals, and newspapers are kept for use.
attendant: 1. Being present, or in the train; accompanying; in waiting. From the attendant flotilla rang notes triumph. Sir W. Scott. Cherub and Seraph . . . attendant on their Lord. Milton. 2. | 1. atlanta: A genus of small glassy heteropod mollusks found swimming at the surface in mid ocean. See Heteropod.
atticize: To conform or make conformable to the language, customs, etc., of Attica. | 1. To side with the Athenians. 2. To use the Attic idiom or style; to conform to the customs or modes of thought of the Athenians.
attenuated: 1. Made thin or slender. 2. Made thin or less viscid; rarefied. Bacon.
atwain: In twain; asunder. [Obs. or Poetic] "Cuts atwain the knots." Tennyson.
atramental: Of or pertaining to ink; inky; black, like ink; as, atramental galls; atramentous spots.
atmology: That branch of science which treats of the laws and phenomena of aqueous vapor. Whewell.
athletics: The art of training by athletic exercises; the games and sports of athletes.
atrabilarian: Affected with melancholy; atrabilious. Arbuthnot. | A person much given to melancholy; a hypochondriac. I. Disraeli.
ataxic: Characterized by ataxy, that is, (a) by great irregularity of functions or symptoms, or (b) by a want of coordinating power in movements. Ataxic fever, malignant typhus fever. Pinel.
atomicity: Degree of atomic attraction; equivalence; valence; also (a later use) the number of atoms in an elementary molecule. See Valence.
attain: 1. To achieve or accomplish, that is, to reach by efforts; to gain; to compass; as, to attain rest. Is he wise who hopes to attain the end without the means Abp. Tillotson. 2. | 1. To come or arrive, by motion, growth, bodily exertion, or efforts toward a place, object, state, etc.; to reach. If by any means they might attain to Phenice. Acts xxvii. 12.
attempt: 1. To make trial or experiment of; to try; to endeavor to do or perform (some action); to assay; as, to attempt to sing; to attempt a bold flight. Something attempted, something done, Has earned a… | To make an attempt; -- with upon. (old) Sir T. Browne.
atmospheric: 1. Of or pertaining to the atmosphere; of the nature of, or resembling, the atmosphere; as, atmospheric air; the atmospheric envelope of the earth. 2. Existing in the atmosphere. attitudinarianism: A practicing of attitudes; posture making.
atavism: (a) The recurrence, or a tendency to a recurrence, of the original type of a species in the progeny of its varieties; resemblance to remote rather than to near ancestors; reversion to the original form. attentate: 1. An attempt; an assault. (old) Bacon. 2. (Law) (a) A proceeding in a court of judicature, after an inhibition is decreed. (b) Any step wrongly innovated or attempted in a suit by an inferior judge.
attenuant: Making thin, as fluids; diluting; rendering less dense and viscid; diluent. -- n. (Med.) A medicine that thins or dilutes the fluids; a diluent.
attemperament: A tempering, or mixing in due proportion.
athermancy: Inability to transmit radiant; impermeability to heat. Tyndall.
atter: Poison; venom; corrupt matter from a sore. (old) Holland.
ateles: A genus of American monkeys with prehensile tails, and having the thumb wanting or rudimentary. See Spider monkey, and Coaita.
atones: Etym: [See At one.] (old) Down he fell atones as a stone. Chaucer.
athetize: To set aside or reject as spurious, as by marking with an obelus.
atmidometer: An instrument for measuring the evaporation from water, ice, or snow. Brande & C.
atmologist: One who is versed in atmology.
atramentaceous: Black, like ink; inky; atramental. (old) Derham.
atwite: To speak reproachfully of; to twit; to upbraid. (old)
attractivity: The quality or degree of attractive power.
attitude: 1. (Paint. & Sculp.) The posture, action, or disposition of a figure or a statue. 2. atomical: 1. Of or pertaining to atoms. 2. Extremely minute; tiny. Atomic philosophy, or Doctrine of atoms, a system which assuming that atoms are endued with gravity and motion accounted thus for the origin and formation of all things.
attractability: The quality or fact of being attractable. Sir W. Jones.
atmometer: An instrument for measuring the rate of evaporation from a moist surface; an evaporometer. Huxley.
attempter: 1. One who attempts; one who essays anything. 2. An assailant; also, a temper. (old)
athenian: Of or pertaining to Athens, the metropolis of Greece. -- n. A native or citizen of Athens.
attache: One attached to another person or thing, as a part of a suite or staff. Specifically: One attached to an embassy.
atokous: Producing only asexual individuals, as the eggs of certain annelids.
atomist: One who holds to the atomic philosophy or theory. Locke.
attacca: Attack at once; -- a direction at the end of a movement to show that the next is to follow immediately, without any pause.
ateletssauce: A sauce (such as egg and bread crumbs) used for covering bits of meat, small birds, or fish, strung on skewers for frying.
atrocious: 1. Extremely heinous; full of enormous wickedness; as, atrocious quilt or deeds. 2. Characterized by, or expressing, great atrocity, great atrocity. atavic: Pertaining to a remote ancestor, or to atavism.
attrition: 1. The act of rubbing together; friction; the act of wearing by friction, or by rubbing substances together; abrasion. Effected by attrition of the inward stomach. Arbuthnot. 2. The state of being worn. Johnson. 3. (Theol.) Grief for sin arising only from fear of punishment or feelings of shame. See Contrition. Wallis.
atonement: 1. (Literally, a setting at one.) Reconciliation; restoration of friendly relations; agreement; concord. (old) By whom we have now received the atonement. Rom. v. 11. He desires to make atonement Betwixt the Duke of Gloucester and your brothers. Shak. 2.
atmolysis: The act or process of separating mingled gases of unequal diffusibility by transmission through porous substances.
attach: 1. To bind, fasten, tie, or connect; to make fast or join; as, to attach one thing to another by a string, by glue, or the like. The shoulder blade is . . . attached only to the muscles. To come into legal operation in connection with anything; to vest;
atrophied: Affected with atrophy, as a tissue or organ; arrested in development at a very early stage; rudimentary.
atomization: 1. The act of reducing to atoms, or very minute particles; or the state of being so reduced. 2. (Med.) The reduction of fluids into fine spray.
attired: Provided with antlers, as a stag.
attendment: An attendant circumstance. (old) The uncomfortable attendments of hell. Sir T. Browne.
atabal: A kettledrum; a kind of tabor, used by the Moors. Croly.
attentive: 1. Heedful; intent; observant; regarding with care or attention. attollent: Lifting up; raising; as, an attollent muscle. Derham.
atrip: (a) Just hove clear of the ground; -said of the anchor. (b) Sheeted home, hoisted taut up and ready for trimming; -- said of sails. (c) Hoisted up and ready to be swayed across; -- said of yards.
atwo: In two; in twain; asunder. (old) Chaucer.
atramentarious: Like ink; suitable for making ink. Sulphate of iron (copperas, green vitriol) is called atramentarious, as being used in making ink.
atheological: Opposed to theology; atheistic. Bp. Montagu.
ation: A suffix forming nouns of action, and often equivalent to the verbal substantive in -ing. It sometimes has the further meanings of state, and that which results from the action. attenuate: 1. To make thin or slender, as by mechanical or chemical action upon inanimate objects, or by the effects of starvation, disease, etc., upon living bodies. 2. attribution: 1. The act of attributing or ascribing, as a quality, character, or function, to a thing or person, an effect to a cause. 2. That which is ascribed or attributed.
atheism: 1. The disbelief or denial of the existence of a God, or supreme intelligent Being. Atheism is a ferocious system, that leaves nothing above us to excite awe, nor around us to awaken tenderness. R. Hall. Atheism and pantheism are often wrongly confounded. Shipley. 2. Godlessness.
atomically: In an atomic manner; in accordance with the atomic philosophy.
atrypa: A extinct genus of Branchiopoda, very common in Silurian limestones.
attitudinize: To assume affected attitudes; to strike an attitude; to pose. Maria, who is the most picturesque figure, was put to attitudinize at the harp. Hannah More.

Atrabiliary arteries, capsules, and veins (Anat.), those pertaining to the kidney;
atheling: An Anglo-Saxon prince or nobleman; esp., the heir apparent or a prince of the royal family. [Written also Adeling and Ætheling.]
attest: 1. To bear witness to; to certify; to affirm to be true or genuine; as, to attest the truth of a writing, a copy of record. Facts . . . attested by particular pagan authors. Addison. 2. | Witness; testimony; attestation. The attest of eyes and ears. Shak.
attrap: To entrap; to insnare. (old) Grafton. | To adorn with trapping; to array. (old) Shall your horse be attrapped . . . more richly Holland.
atman: (a) The life principle, soul, or individual essence. (b) The universal ego from whom all individual atmans arise. This sense is a European excrescence on the East Indian thought.
athletic: 1. Of or pertaining to athletes or to the exercises practiced by them; as, athletic games or sports. 2. Befitting an athlete; strong; muscular; robust; vigorous; as, athletic Celts. "Athletic soundness." South. -- Ath*let"ic*al*ly, adv.

atmo: The standard atmospheric pressure used in certain physical measurements calculations; conventionally, that pressure under which the barometer stands at 760 millimeters, at a temperature of 0º Centigrade, at the level of the sea, and in the latitude of Paris. Sir W. Thomson.
atechnic: Without technical or artistic knowledge. Difficult to convey to the atechnic reader. Etching & Engr.
athamaunt: Adamant. (old) Written in the table of athamaunt. Chaucer.
atheroid: Shaped like an ear of grain.
atterrate: To fill up with alluvial earth. (old) Ray.

attrectation: Frequent handling or touching. (old) Jer. Taylor.
atlaspowder: A blasting powder or dynamite composed of nitroglycerin, wood fiber, sodium nitrate, and magnesium carbonate.
attender: One who, or that which, attends.
attaminate: To corrupt; to defile; to contaminate. (old) Blount.
attachment: 1. The act attaching, or state of being attached; close adherence or affection; fidelity; regard; anas, an attachment to a friend, or to a party. 2. attaste: To taste or cause to taste. (old) Chaucer.
attract: 1. To draw to, or cause to tend to; esp. to cause to approach, adhere, or combine; or to cause to resist divulsion, separation, or decomposition. All bodies and all parts of bodies mutually attract themselves and one another. Derham. 2. To draw by influence of a moral or emotional kind; to engage or fix, as the mind, attention, etc.; to invite or allure;
atmospherical: 1. Of or pertaining to the atmosphere; of the nature of, or resembling, the atmosphere; as, atmospheric air; the atmospheric envelope of the earth. 2. Existing in the atmosphere. The lower atmospheric current. Darwin. 3. Caused, or operated on, by the atmosphere; as, an atmospheric effect; an atmospheric engine. 4. Dependent on the atmosphere.
atypical: That has no type; devoid of typical character; irregular; unlike the type.
attainableness: The quality of being attainable; attainability.
attend: 1. To direct the attention to; to fix the mind upon; to give heed to; to regard. (old) The diligent pilot in a dangerous tempest doth not attend the unskillful words of the passenger. Sir P. Sidney. | 1. To apply the mind, or pay attention, with a view to perceive, understand, or comply; to pay regard; to heed; to listen; -- usually followed by to. Attend to the voice of my supplications. Ps.
athalamous: Not furnished with shields or beds for the spores, as the thallus of certain lichens.
attent: Attentive; heedful. (old) Let thine ears be attent unto the prayer. 2 Chron. vi. 40. | Attention; heed. (old) Spenser.
attracter: One who, or that which, attracts.
attic: Of or pertaining to Attica, in Greece, or to Athens, its principal city; marked by such qualities as were characteristic of the Athenians; classical; refined. Attic base (Arch.), a peculiar form of… | 1. (Arch.) (a) A low story above the main order or orders of a facade, in the classical styles; -- a term introduced in the 17th century. Hence: (b) A room or rooms behind that part of the exterior;
attorney: 1. A substitute; a proxy; an agent. (old) And will have no attorney but myself. Shak. 2. (Law) (a) One who is legally appointed by another to transact any business for him; an attorney in fact. | To perform by proxy; to employ as a proxy. (old) Shak.
atmolyze: To subject to atmolysis; to separate by atmolysis.
atomy: An atom; a mite; a pigmy. | A skeleton. [Ludicrous] Shak.
athirst: 1. Wanting drink; thirsty. 2. Having a keen appetite or desire; eager; longing. "Athirst for battle." Cowper.
at: Primarily, this word expresses the relations of presence, nearness in place or time, or direction toward; as, at the ninth hour; at the house; to aim at a mark. It is less definite than in or on; at the house may be in or near the house. From this original import are derived all the various uses of at. It expresses: - 1.
atherine: A small marine fish of the family Atherinidæ, having a silvery stripe along the sides. The European species (Atherina presbyter) is used as food. The American species (Menidia notata) is called silversides and sand smelt. See Silversides.
ataraxy: Perfect peace of mind, or calmness.
attame: 1. To pierce; to attack. (old) 2. To broach; to begin. And right anon his tale he hath attamed. Chaucer.
atacamite: An oxychloride of copper, usually in emerald-green prismatic crystals.
attainment: 1. The act of attaining; the act of arriving at or reaching; hence, the act of obtaining by efforts. The attainment of every desired object. Sir W. Jones. 2. That which is attained to, or obtained by exertion; acquirement; acquisition; (pl.), mental acquirements; knowledge; as, literary and scientific attainments.
attrite: 1. Rubbed; worn by friction. Milton. 2. (Theol.) Repentant from fear of punishment; having attrition of grief for sin; -- opposed to contrite.
atlantic: 1. Of or pertaining to Mt. Atlas in Libya, and hence applied to the ocean which lies between Europe and Africa on the east and America on the west; as, the Atlantic Ocean (called also the Atlantic); the Atlantic basin; the Atlantic telegraph. 2. Of or pertaining to the isle of Atlantis. 3. Descended from Atlas. The seven Atlantic sisters. Milton.
ataunto: Fully rigged, as a vessel; with all sails set; set on end or set right.
atheous: 1. Atheistic; impious. (old) Milton. 2. Without God, neither accepting nor denying him. I should say science was atheous, and therefore could not be atheistic. Bp. of Carlisle.
attribute: To ascribe; to consider (something) as due or appropriate (to); to refer, as an effect to a cause; to impute; to assign; to consider as belonging (to). We attribute nothing to God that hath any… | 1. That which is attributed; a quality which is considered as belonging to, or inherent in, a person or thing; an essential or necessary property or characteristic.
attercop: 1. A spider. (old) 2. A peevish, ill-natured person. [North of Eng.]
attorn: 1. (Feudal Law) To turn, or transfer homage and service, from one lord to another. This is the act of feudatories, vassals, or tenants, upon the alienation of the estate. Blackstone. 2. (Modern Law) To agree to become tenant to one to whom reversion has been granted.
attachable: Capable of being attached; esp., liable to be taken by writ or precept.
atheist: 1. One who disbelieves or denies the existence of a God, or supreme intelligent Being. 2. A godless person. (old) Syn. -- Infidel; unbeliever. Note: See Infidel.
atop: On or at the top. Milton.
atresia: Absence or closure of a natural passage or channel of the body; imperforation.
atrocha: A kind of chætopod larva in which no circles of cilia are developed.
atterration: The act of filling up with earth, or of forming land with alluvial earth. (old)
ataraxia: Perfect peace of mind, or calmness.
atomism: The doctrine of atoms. See Atomic philosophy, under Atomic.
athecata: A division of Hydroidea in which the zooids are naked, or not inclosed in a capsule. See Tubularian.
atrede: To surpass in council. (old) Men may the olde atrenne, but hat atrede. Chaucer.
atrial: Of or pertaining to an atrium.
athetosis: A variety of chorea, marked by peculiar tremors of the fingers and toes.
attle: Rubbish or refuse consisting of broken rock containing little or no ore. Weale.
